newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Violence in Belgrade as OSCE backs opposition. [CORRECTED 13:21 GMT 28/12]
newsitem.headline: Violence in Belgrade as OSCE backs opposition. [CORRECTED 13:21 GMT 28/12]

text.p: Anti-government demonstrators and riot police clashed on Friday after an opposition protest rally in Belgrade as Europe's top security body backed Serbian opposition claims it was robbed of local election victories.

Independent media reported that 29 people had been injured in skirmishes between baton-wielding police and people leaving the scene of the opposition demonstration. At least one person was beaten unconscious, eyewitnesses said.

The violence, some of the worst in almost six weeks of daily protests against President Slobodan Milosevic and the government, came hours after the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) threw its support behind claims that the Serbian opposition had won disputed local elections.
In a report the OSCE confirmed the opposition Zajedno coalition had won elections in key districts.

The OSCE delegation came to Belgrade at Milosevic's invitation to investigate the November 17 poll which touched off the cycle of protests which have brought out up to 200,000 people daily on to the streets.
Milosevic's foreign minister, Milan Milutinovic, welcomed the report as "considered and balanced", without mentioning the OSCE's main recommendation to accept the opposition victories.
But he said the OSCE mission had confused several facts, including the number of disputed districts.

"What is important is the joint list of the (ruling) Socialist Party, JUL (Yugoslav Left) and New Democracy won the majority of votes in all other municipalities," he told the state news agency Tanjug.
In the violence, at least one person was beaten unconscious, and a man who said he was walking home from a medical conference received an open head wound, eyewitnesses said.
A mother and her 12-year-old daughter were caught in the skirmishes and slightly injured, and three foreign television crews were attacked and had their cameras smashed.
A reporter from the independent Radio Index said: "It seems riot police are intervening in response to jeering. No other provocation took place."

Milutinovic said: "The report confirms that the elections were held in the most regular manner and that the majority of people were able to express their voice," he said. (Corrects to make clear that Milutinovic is source for quote and not Radio Index reporter.)

Former Spanish Prime Minister Filipe Gonzalez who led the OSCE delegation said he had concluded that the Zajedno coalition had fairly won the local polls in 13 key provincial centres as well as in Belgrade's municipalities.
Gonzalez told a Geneva news conference that the reasons given by the Serbian courts for annulling the opposition victories were based on arguments "that no democratic country could have accepted".
Soon after Gonzalez announced his verdict in Geneva, the news spread to Belgrade and opposition supporters participating in Friday's demonstration.
The crowd of some 80,000 danced in jubilation and cheered the OSCE report, which added weight to mounting international demands that Milosevic respect democracy.
But opposition leaders were sceptical that Milosevic would respond positively to the Gonzalez report.
"We do not expect him to accept the findings of this commission. We expect further escalation, aggravation of this political crisis," said Zoran Djindjic, leader of the opposition Democratic Party.
The United States welcomed Gonzalez's conclusions and called on Milsoveic to accept the opposition's victories.

The State Department said Gonzalez's conclusions "match our own" and Serbia "must honour international commitments and move toward democracy before it can be accepted fully into the international community."

Italian foreign minister Lamberto Dini, who has held talks with the government and opposition separately, urged Belgrade "to respect the OSCE's recommendations, expecially regarding the towns where the vote results were annulled".
Zajedno's marches had continued for more than five weeks without serious incident until Milosevic's Socialist party organised its own counter-rally sparking a wave of street violence.

On Thursday, riot police enforced an Interior Ministry decree banning demonstrations which distrupted traffic, by forcing the protesters onto pedestrian malls and footpaths -- a tactic repeated on Friday.
